You should try the following : check your connection, disable ad-blocker, clear your browser cache, try in private mode, try from another browser/computer/connection. 0 CATAN The Settlers of Catan, Die Siedler von Catan, Les Colons de Catane First published in Germany in 1995 as Die Siedler von CATAN, then in English as The Settlers of CATAN in 1996, CATAN celebrates its 25th anniversary in 2020. To begin the game, you build the game board using hexagonal terrain tiles. Catan is born - a beautiful island with mountains, pastures, hills, fields, and forests, surrounded by the sea. Each of you places two small houses on spaces where three terrain hexes meet. They are your starting settlements. And so it begins. The starting player rolls two dice. An “11!” Each terrain hex is marked with a number. Each player who owns a settlement adjacent to a terrain hex marked with the number rolled receives a resource produced by this hex. Hills produce brick, forests produce lumber, mountains produce ore, fields produce grain, and pastures produce wool. You use these resources to expand across Catan: you build roads and new settlements or upgrade your existing settlements to cities. For example, a road costs 1 brick and 1 lumber. If you do not have the necessary resources, you can acquire them by trading with your opponents. Each settlement is worth 1 victory point and each city is worth 2 victory points. If you expand cleverly, you may be the first player to reach 10 victory points and thus win the game! Number of players: 3 - 4 Game duration: 35 mn Complexity: 2 / 5 Play CATAN and 1414 other games online. No download necessary - play directly from your web browser. With your friends and thousands of players from the whole world. Free. Discover Board Game Arena Designer Klaus Teuber Artist Eric Hibbeler, Quentin Regnes, Michael Menzel (former edition) Publisher Catan - Year 1995 Developed by darhf , lordalx Maintained by Number of games played 8 961 562 Number of players 3 - 4 Game duration 35 mn Complexity 2 Strategy 3 Luck 3 Interaction 4 Available since Jun 22nd 2022 Release 261025-1142 Play CATAN and 1414 other games online. No download necessary - play directly from your web browser. With your friends and thousands of players from the whole world. Free. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Objective 2 Setup 3 Gameplay 4 Scoring 5 End of Game 6 Variants 6.1 Cities & Knights 6.1.1 Event Dice 6.1.2 Cities 6.1.3 Variants Objective Get resources to buy various buildings and development cards, and try to be the first player to reach 10 points (or 13 in case of City & Knights) Setup The board consists of hills (brick), forest (lumber), mountains (ore), fields (grain), pasture (wool) and a desert (nothing) at random places. Each terrain except the desert has a number of 2-12 on it. The desert starts with the robber on it. Each player places 2 settlements and 1 road next to each settlement on the board, then they receive resources for each terrain around the second settlement. Gameplay Rolling for resource production (obligatory): On your turn, roll 2 dice and calculate the sum. The terrains with that number produce resources for all players who have settlements or cities next to them (if the robber isn't blocking them): 1 resource per settlement and 2 per city. If you roll a 7, no one gets any resources and players with 8 resources or more must discard half of them (rounded down). You must move the robber to a new terrain and steal 1 random resource from a player who has a settlement or city next to that terrain. Trading (optional): during your turn you can trade resources with all other players ( domestic trade ) with the bank ( maritime trade ) at the standard rate of 4 identical resources for 1 or at a preferential rate of a harbour if you have a settlement next to it. Building (optional): finally, you can build roads and settlements, upgrade settlements to cities or purchase a development card by paying the resources needed. Roads must connect to the initial settlements and cost 1 brick + 1 lumber (worth 0 points) Settlements must be connected by roads to existing settlements (except at start) and cost 1 brick + 1 lumber + 1 wool + 1 grain (worth 1 point) Cities replace an existing settlement and cost 3 ore + 2 grain (worth 2 points) Development cards (unavailable in Cities & Knights) cost 1 ore + 1 wool + 1 grain and include 14 Knight cards that allow to move the robber to another terrain and steal a resource 2 Road Building cards allowing extra roads to be built 2 Year of Plenty cards providing two free resources of choice 2 Monopoly cards giving all other players that help gathering resources or building road•s 5 Victory Point cards You can play a development card at any time during your turn, even before rolling the dice, as long as it was bought on a previous turn and is not a victory card. This is an expansion for CATAN. Players can build shipping lanes, which are very similar to roads. Additionally, the game comes with many different water-hex-heavy variant setups. The English version (CATAN Studio) should only be used with the English base game, instead of the German one (Kosmos), because of matching components. The Kosmos German version should only be used with the German base game. Additionally, several different editions exist; 5th edition is the most recent. Editions should only be used with same edition, otherwise the purchase of adapter kit is required.

Part of the Catan Series.

This game requires CATAN.  Ideally, using the same publisher and edition of the game.

[Rating: 2/10] Don't bother.  The new additions simply don't add much to the game beyond playtime.  It feels like the original, with unnecessary distracting crap thrown in.  The epitome of what I DON'T want an expansion to be.  [url=http://www.boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/926]Cities & Knights[/url] is a much better expansion.

[Rating: 2/10] The more but smaller islands provide a bigger but more spread map, which results in more drawbacks than it's worth: * more cities border the sea => less efficiency/resource-income => slower start * cities further apart => more cost to connect * players are more spread => less tension in getting certain spots  All this combines into a longer game that has less player interaction. The other expansions offer more variety in gameplay with less re-inventing the game.  My wife even started to hate sea-themed board games because of this expansion. It got better in the last months, but I still have to

[Rating: 2/10] The unknown hexes that players can venture towards add another layer of randomness which can throw a wrench into a well executed gameplan or allow a haphazard gameplan to stumble into victory.   Personally, I found that this accentuates what I didn't like about Catan (the degree to which luck determines the outcome, rather than skillful play)

[Rating: 2/10] 220927 It makes Catan a little bigger but lacks innovation. A must to try, though. A first step to Expansions

[Rating: 2.5/10] Likes: About the only thing this offers is the gold tiles.  Dislikes: The sea tiles and thinning of the map just drags the game out. The trade/boat routes don't really offer much more.

[Rating: 3/10] Only played once - and I did'nt even have a go at it. So its heresay knowledge. Guess I'll never get to play this one. Keep it to complete my colection.

[Rating: 3/10] I love regular Settlers and Knights and Cities even more. This version, however, add no new fun over and above what you get with Settlers, but drastically adds to the setup and teardown time.  I would never choose this over regular Settlers or K&C

[Rating: 3/10] The added set up time and the scenarios just didn't do much to improve Settlers for me.  Cities and Knights is a much better expansion.

[Rating: 3/10] Takes what little I like about Settlers and ruins it.  I simply won't play with this set.

[Rating: 3/10] I like Settlers and Cities and Knights, but this expansion added very little in our games with it other than additional reading and setup time.  It has gold tiles.  That is about all the good I can say about it.

[Rating: 3/10] Doesn't add a lot to the basic game. Makes the game playable with 4 with the increased space, and gives you some room for variation to freshen it up. That said,  I think the complaint that it adds length without depth is fair. The option of much more random maps and the exploration variant are worthy additions in the abstract, but the reality of the implementation is not to my liking. I rarely get the urge to play Siedler anymore, and even more rarely with this expansion as the game plays at least 30-60 minutes longer because of the lack of 3 intersection hexes and longer roads/shipping lanes.

[Rating: 3/10] Hard for me to justify the added time this gives the game. Also it requires more than 2 players.

[Rating: 3/10] Owned the Mayfair 3rd edition (the one printed in 1998). In Jan 2014, I traded this and Cities & Knights of Catan and the 5-6 player expansions for both in return for Liberte and Perikles.  This one was a classic case of making an expansion for a game that didn't need one.  Still enjoy Settlers greatly, but its expansions were wasted on my groups.

[Rating: 3/10] Own Kosmos edition. It doesn't add much to regular Catan and rather prolongs the game in unnecessarily way. The main addition to the game is ships which are nothing but mobile roads on the ocean. It doesn't even travel. Not exciting at all. Only reason I have this is so that I can play some of the neat Senarios in Catan Book.

[Rating: 3/10] Doesn't add enough to justify its cost.  I haven't played with solely the Seafarer's expansion (typically with Cities and Knights as well), but I'd almost prefer to play normal Settlers.  Priced as much as the base game, I would never purchase Seafarers.  Maybe my rating is unfair, but I'm not sure if it adds anything particularly significant.  Only doubles the cost of the game.

[Rating: 3/10] As an expansion, it just added complexity and the game took a longer time to play. I did not enjoy playing with the expansion.

[Rating: 3/10] Seafarers allows for more scenario options, but otherwise I don't feel it adds much to the game at all. While C&K really gives you something more to chew on, Seafarers feels like nothing more than roads on water.

[Rating: 3/10] I love the visual aesthetics of building roads and shipping lanes.  The exploration scenarios carry no interst for me because the land tiles are so limited and mundane that there is no thrill in the discovery.

[Rating: 3/10] Game in a Nutshell: Expansion that creates water stretches that need to be crossed using boats to get to more settle-able land.  Played as: 3 and 4 player  Pros: The idea of sailing from one island to the next felt exciting.  Cons: I got pissed that it was the person who stuck to the biggest island, never sailed/ explored much, always ended up winning. I think you'd hope for an expansion to add something to a game, this seemed to break it.  Other: As I remember, there is a set up or two that has more, but smaller islands scattered around. [Rating: 3/10] Didn't seem to add much to the original Settlers.  I can't say it made the game worse, but why spend money to buy an expansion if it doesn't make the game better (or at least more interesting?) A big disappointment.
